utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, registrar. Mr. Oric, can you receive interpretation in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you. You may sit down. Appearances, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I am Patricia Sellers representing the Prosecution, with co-counsel Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and our case manager, Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you Ms. Sellers, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, together with Mr. John Jones. I appear on behalf of Mr. Naser Oric. Joining us today are our legal assistant, Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you. Any preliminary matters? Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just one which concerns the scheduling and time estimates for witnesses. We've received an amended witness list and it occurs to us that it seems the Prosecution isn't building into their scheduling allowance, or sufficient allowance for the time for us to cross-examine witnesses. And by way of example, today for Ratko Nikolic, the estimated time of testimony is three hours, and then we have three hours for the witness tomorrow. That would leave us after housekeeping matters with half an hour for cross-examination. We've said from the start as a general rule we need about as much time for cross-examination as the Prosecution need for examination-in-chief. In fact, I think we've been shorter than that with the exception of Dr. Gow which was exceptional. But, for example, with today's witness I'll need three hours two and a half, three hours. And with the Prosecution scheduling a witness every day but at the same time planning to spend three hours in examination-in-chief means we won't have time for cross-examination but we will seem to be at blame when we run over. So we would ask the Prosecution in their scheduling make allowance for the fact that we need virtually as much time in cross-examination as they need for examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That makes much sense to me. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Absolutely. If there's an error creeping into our scheduling, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It has been there for quite some time, actually. The only reason why we could manage is that it was taking less time than anticipated -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- both for the direct and the cross. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand that and I certainly don't -- the Prosecution certainly doesn't want to deprive the Defence for their rightful time for cross-examination. We'll bear that in mind and ensure that our scheduling takes more into -- the Defence's requirements more comprehensively into account. We'll deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with this one first. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Today's witness, who will be leading? MR. DI FAZIO: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And how much time do you think you require? MR. DI FAZIO: On paper, it's -- it will take me -- I would have thought about two hours. With this particular witness, knowing -- having spoken to him, it's going to be slower than one would normally expect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So the chances are there is more than a slight chance that we will have this witness again tomorrow morning. MR. DI FAZIO: I'd say there's a pretty good chance of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then there is the next one which was scheduled -- MR. DI FAZIO: I don't have the list before me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not mentioning names because the list that I have doesn't show whether they are protected witnesses or not, so I'm not taking any chances. Then you have the next one, which is also on paper -- this person was scheduled for today originally. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And again I see three hours here. Who will be in charge of that witness? MR. DI FAZIO: Mr. Wubben will be, I assume. Yes, yes -- no, I'm sorry. I apologise. That's Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: And then the next one is Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. And Mr. Jones or Madam Vidovic, the next two witnesses, the one which is scheduled for today but which we will hear tomorrow and the -- then the following one which is scheduled -- was originally scheduled for tomorrow, which we will --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, well, I would think for today's witness that I would probably need around two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the others?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Two hours until the next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two hours, the next one?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the one after him?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me just check, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Two and a half hours for the one after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it seems clear to me, Mr. Di Fazio, that the witness who was scheduled originally for Friday, Friday the 9th, I don't think you should even try to bring him over if he is not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because if -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm informed that two are here, which basically means one -- two. And another two are coming today. What's the big idea of bringing someone today if he or she will not be testifying before today, today -- week? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, well that wouldn't be very sensible, I agree, if Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Apart from the expense. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The flight remains the same. MR. DI FAZIO: Can I confer and find out exactly what the position is with my colleagues regarding witnesses, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If Your Honours please, it's worked out that way. We've had some delays in the case with various issues arising from time to time and we'll try to work on the basis of one witness a day or thereabouts. So we've been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What happened with this -- much, but there you are. I mean, this witness has been here since Tuesday of last week. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, that is so, if Your Honours please. But we did expect to go faster on Friday and we had the problems of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you couldn't go faster on Friday, neither one Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond nor the either. MR. DI FAZIO: But this has happened, but I understand what Your Honour is saying and we can try and ensure that we don't bring them in so fast and be a little more flexible. I'm alive to the issue and I'll speak to the team about that and we'll make sure that we try and keep them -- get them in closer to their anticipated time of giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It seems, Mr. Di Fazio, that there's no way we can deal with more than three witnesses in the course of this week. This one plus another two. On the 8th we have plenary. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, I -- we had been trying I think in accordance with the Trial Chamber's witnesses to try and get through one a day, at least with crime-based witnesses, and it just doesn't always work out that way for various reasons and I think that's been creeping in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, you know what the problem is and try to make adjustments accordingly. MR. DI FAZIO: We will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The reason why I'm saying is this is -- keeping someone here for an entire week without being called to give evidence, it's costly, especially if the person comes with the entire family, as sometimes happens with certain protected witnesses and I suppose also frustrating. I mean, it would be frustrating to me at least. I don't know whether they enjoy being here in The Hague, which is a lovely city. But ... MR. DI FAZIO: I think it has been going reasonably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The tourist is one thing and waiting to give testimony is another. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I think it has been going reasonably smoothly. What you say is correct about this last witness. That shouldn't happen. And as I said and the only thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I think we've been doing really fine. I think we have been doing really fine. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But when I see three hours, three hours, et cetera, Mr. Jones is right. MR. DI FAZIO: I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't work on the assumption that I give you three hours and then give them what's left. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have to allow -- what I can do is, if my colleagues agree, is to say: Okay, you have three hours 45 minutes every sitting. Divide them equally by -- share them -- divide the time equally amongst you or between you. That's the only thing. But then there are some witnesses where you can do that, no harm ensues. And there are some other witnesses that are so important, either for the Prosecution or for the Defence or for us, that cutting down on the time allotted will be a mistake. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll personally undertake to review the remaining witnesses before Christmas this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll do that myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: And I'll give you my assessment of what's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And thank you, Mr. Jones, for raising the matter because it has been on my mind as well. Any further preliminaries? MR. DI FAZIO: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see none. Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to make sure that you are receiving interpretation in our own language. Please confirm that you are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are about to start giving yesterday. And before you do so, according or pursuant to our rules you need to enter a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath that -- or to the effect that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The lady standing beside you who is our usher is going to hand you the text of the solemn declaration. Please read it out loud and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal, that you will be testifying the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please sit down. You are now going to be asked a set of questions by Mr. Di Fazio, whom you've met already. In your own interest, I suggest to you that you be as brief as possible in your answers. And if the question calls for a yes or no answer, then you just answer yes or no without going into any details unless you are asked to go into details otherwise you will be here for days and days. When Mr. Di Fazio finishes with his questions, then Mr. Jones, who is appearing for Naser Oric, will cross-examine you. He will put to you a set of questions, which you also have a responsibility to answer. There is one thing I need to make clear to you, namely that you have no right to distinguish between the questions being asked by the Prosecution and the questions put to you by the Defence. Both the Prosecution and the Defence have a right to put questions to you as a witness, and you have, pursuant to the solemn declaration that you entered this morning, a solemn duty to answer each question truthfully and fully, irrespective of who is putting it to you. Did I make myself clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So then we can start. Mr. Di Fazio, he is all yours. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if you see that he is running at a tangent, please get him back into the fold straight away yourself. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, I will do my best, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Nikolic, I just want to put some personal details to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can lead him there. MR. DI FAZIO: I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to put some personal details to you and then you can tell me if they're correct by simply telling yes or no. You were a Serb of Serb ethnicity, you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please speak into the microphone otherwise we can't hear you. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll start again and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are of Serb ethnicity. You were born in the small village of Opravdici, which is in the municipality of Bratunac, and you were born there in 1945. You're also known as Pajo. You're married and your wife's name is Marija. You have two sons, Goran and Zoran and you've never been a member of a political party --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before he answers yes or no. This Pajo, is he also known as Pajo or was -- his father's name was Pajo? MR. DI FAZIO: Ah, yes. I'm very grateful to Your Honours for Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll alter the details. Your father's name was Pajo and you've never been a member of a political party. Now, are all those details correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about particulars that applied -- personal particulars that applied to you in 1992 and 1993. Again, you were living in a small hamlet calls Zonjici which is close to Opravdici. Up until the 1st of May, 1992, you worked as a watchman, a night watchman, or a watchman at a company called the 21st of May company. And thereafter for the remainder of 1992 and very early 1993 you continued to work on your farm, which is just near Zonjici. All of those details correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your farm was about 16 Hectares and had chicken, cattle, sheep, sometimes grew wheat, flax, it had houses and outbuildings and barns on the farm. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you some questions about the geography of your area. Can you tell the Trial Chamber the distance from the small hamlet of Zonjici to Siljkovici, Kravica and Opravdici. If I were to stand in your hamlet of Zonjici, how far away would those three villages and hamlets be, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The distance is one and a half kilometres from Kravica; as the crow flies, perhaps as far as 4 or 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the other two hamlets, Siljkovici and Opravdici?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Opravdici are just above Zonjici. The distance is 1 kilometre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I stood in Zonjici, would I have a clear view of the hamlet of Siljkovici?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want you to look at a map that I produce to you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, these have got arrows on them, but nothing else, no other writings or anything on them. I don't think it's in contention that these towns or hamlets exist. And I only want to give the map to provide a sort of perspective to the Trial Chamber. Perhaps if they can be put on the ELMO very briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, all I want you to do, Mr. Nikolic, is look over at this map which I think you've seen before, and point out these three -- three little hamlets and villages that are spoken of, Opravdici, Kravica, and Siljkovici. Do you see those?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Opravdici --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Mr. Nikolic, Mr. Nikolic --

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can't see it here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. Mr. Nikolic -- all right. Have a look there. Can you see them?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Witness complies].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Siljkovici.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Witness complies].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I'll tender that into evidence. Yes, and could it be provided with an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will -- being tendered, received, and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P45 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, P453.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 453. 453. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, I hate to interrupt Your Honour. It's just that my learned friend was also asking the distance from Zonjici to Siljkovici. And since he put to him that it was -- there was a clear view of Siljkovici from Zonjici, I think we should have an answer from the witness as to how far it is from Zonjici to Siljkovici, because he hasn't answered that question which was put to him yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you put the question again, please, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm grateful to Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The distance between Zonjici and Siljkovici, can you tell us that? 18

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The distance between Zonjici and Siljkovici is not more than -- because Kravica is a bit lower down, so the distance as the crow flies would be about 400 metres. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment and may I look at the exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment. What's the distance as the crow flies between Kravica and Siljkovici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The distance between Kravica and Siljkovici, Siljkovici is a bit higher up and Kravica is a bit lower down. As the crow flies, the line would be vertical. Siljkovici is higher up and Kravica is lower down. If you look down that vertical line, I think the distance would be 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So -- and Zonjici then is -- how far is it from Kravica, Zonjici, as the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between Zonjici and Kravica are the distances not more than 300 metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically in other words between Siljkovici and Kravica the distance is of the width of this room times 2? Double the width of this room? Yeah, because 100 metres. What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As Kravica is in a valley, that's the direction. Because Kravica is broken up and up on the hills there is Siljkovici. And so it's a vertical line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically what you're telling me is that as the crow flies, if one were to draw a line from Siljkovici to Zonjici, it's just 300, 400 metres you're saying, 400 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't tell you exactly but Siljkovici is up here and then Kravica is down there and then there is Zonjici up there, so that's the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's less than half a kilometre in other words. I mean -- all right. I hope we'll be able to see this when we go on-site. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes, yes, Your Honours. There's just one other matter. Do you Your Honours see Zonjici there on the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course I see Zonjici. MR. DI FAZIO: I just wanted to make sure that the Trial Chamber could see that -- see it and I don't need to lead the witness on that. Thank you very much. I'm finished with the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. 453, this map. The map that has been exhibited, 453. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992 and very early 1993, did you own a weapon, a gun, of any type?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you a question about village guards. Was there a village guard in Zonjici, a village guard system of any sort or description at all?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many households were there in the hamlet of Zonjici?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Only two, myself and my relative Milovan. And four others had already moved out of the village several years before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber if you're aware of there being village guards or any sort of guarding system in existence in Opravdici, Siljkovici, and Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are not receiving interpretation into B/C/S. It's possible that the witness is not receiving interpretation either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, for raising that. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure that interpretation is arriving now, is reaching you now? Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to repeat your question, Mr. Di Fazio, please. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was this: Were you -- did you know of any village guard or village guard system operating in those hamlets of -- of Opravdici, Siljkovici, and Kravica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I know that Siljkovici were at the edge along the forest, but not in Opravdici and Zonjici. So in Siljkovici, probably yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what that consisted of, what sort of guard system they had in Siljkovici?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That was the village guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, okay. But you told the Trial Chamber -- you told -- explain to the Judges what -- what that actually means. What is the village guard? What did you know about it? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I heard about the village guards from people. They were guarding the village. They were elderly men for the most part trying to prevent groups of unknown persons turning up. Because had that happened, the women and children would have been in danger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about Kravica? Are you aware of there being any village guard system in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such system in Kravica. But that's what I think. I didn't see anything like that but I wouldn't be able to tell you, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let's just return briefly to your work in 1992. Were you issued with a gun for the purposes of carrying out your duties as a watchman, a pistol?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the company I worked for, yes, a pistol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the close of your shift, would you return it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the last date that you worked at in your company, the 21st of May company?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I worked there until early May I think. Then I was due to have an operation. I have documents to show this. And after that, I was on sick leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you indeed bring along a document to The Hague and show it to me in -- last week concerning that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at this document I produce to you. Is this the document you showed me dealing with your sickness or illness from 1992? Have a look at the document. You can look at it. Turn it around and look at the document. You have the B/C/S version in front of you. Is that the document -- is that a copy of the document you showed me?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. It says you had a hernia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who gave you that piece of paper with that writing on it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The doctor in Mali Zvornik gave it to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the doctor or the nurse?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it says you weren't competent for military service until the end of your treatment. Why did the doctor write that, do you know?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Because I had hernia and I couldn't use my right leg. I had to have surgery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you in fact have surgery in 1992 or not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you continue to suffer from your complaint in 1992 or was it cured?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. I suffered from my complaint, yes. I was not cured. I was still sick.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I seek to tender the medical certificate into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Shall I follow the same sequence as before? Registrar, please, 454. So this document is being tendered, received, and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P454. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992 and early 1993, were you a member of VRS or the JNA or any TO, Territorial Defence, organisation in your area?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you're aware, were you conscripted in 1992 or very early 1993?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you conscripted? Did the army send you a notice or a piece of paper or tell you that you had to go and fight for them, work with them?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to turn your attention to the 7th of January, 1993. On that occasion, were you at home in Zonjici?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your son Zoran also at home?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had your son suffered any sort of injury some time before the 7th of January?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had he been hospitalised?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In Loznica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on this day, the 7th of January, 1993, had he been recently released from hospital or had he been out of hospital for some time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He hadn't been released, but he was allowed to go home for Christmas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the Serb Orthodox Christmas?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your wife at home on the morning of the 7th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it snowing?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It had been snowing before. I know there was about 10 centimetres of snow on the ground. I don't know if it was actually snowing that morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen on that morning?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We were asleep in the room. Marija went outside and started shouting, "Ratko, get up, there's an attack." I said, "What sort of an attack? It's 5.30." You could hear shooting from Siljkovici. I got up. We're on a little hill, as I was trying to explain, so the bullets were whizzing by. We could see fires starting, but we couldn't see while it was still dark. When it started growing light you could see troops going from Srebrenica and Siljkovici toward Kravica burning whatever they could get their hands on. My wife suggested we should flee from the house. We would get killed. My son had been injured, he'd been in Loznica, so we went in the direction of Popovici and the River Drina to get closer to Serbia. I was hit by a bullet in the left leg. I still have the consequences of that. I went with them as far as Popovici, and then I couldn't go on. My son -- my son's left leg was injured. My wife was weeping. I decided to go back. They couldn't carry me, so how could I go on? I decided to go back and be killed in my own home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. I just want to take you back to some of the events you saw before you fled and were shot. Could you see eventually Siljkovici? I'm now talking about the period of time after the attack started. Could you actually see it with your eyes?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, you could see Siljkovici burning. You could see the flames.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is this flames from houses in Siljkovici?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber, thinking back, how much of Siljkovici was burning when you saw it, when you looked at it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Siljkovici is on a hill, so you could see it. You could see flames. It wasn't light yet but you could see the flames in the dark; they were red. You could see the flames rising up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want you to do is tell the Trial Chamber if you could see the flames rising up from one house or more than one house or -- and try and give the Trial Chamber an idea of how much of Siljkovici was burning, whether it was just a small part or half of it or all of it so the Judges understand how much of the town was on fire, the hamlet of Siljkovici.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You could see many flames and lots of smoke. I couldn't judge whether all of Siljkovici was burning, but you could see a lot of fires and a lot of smoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the same time you could see fires and burning and smoke, could you hear the sound of gunfire?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see soldiers moving --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have the problem again. The witness referred to "troops," I'm not sure what that was in the original Bosnian-Hercegovinian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He just wants to complicate matters more, Mr. Jones. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could just describe who he saw and what they were wearing, that way we'll avoid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's a better approach, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you actually see from where you were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see from where you were in Zonjici the men that you have described as soldiers. Could you actually --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He didn't refer to men, didn't refer to soldiers. He said "troops." The whole suggestion which I think Your Honour adopted was that he should simply say who he saw and what they were wearing, and not suggest they were men or soldiers or anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We had -- I don't know, I don't think you were present last Friday when we had this discussion. MR. DI FAZIO: I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were, okay. So basically what I would suggest is you go back to the witness and refer him to when he mentioned or used the word "troops," and ask him to explain. I'm sure he will explain and then you can use the word that he will use to describe "troops," what he meant by troops and the rest of your testimony or at least as far as it relates to this incident, this part of the event. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you clearly see the people you have referred to as "troops"?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I saw people coming down. They had weapons. Whether it was an army or not, but they did have weapons and they were setting fire to places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I couldn't see what they were wearing, whether it was a -- camouflage uniforms were not, I couldn't notice that. I couldn't observe it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you see men moving around Kravica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When they got down from Siljkovici, they went to Kravica. And they had already started burning Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see fires and smoke in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see any men who were armed moving around Kravica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that at the same time as you heard gunfire?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. When they were going down from Siljkovici to Kravica, you could hear them yelling, "Assault," "Go forward."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you actually hear their voices?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember the sort of things they were saying, apart from, "Go forward"?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I remember well. I heard them saying, "Charge, charge. Catch the Chetniks alive."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, I want you to turn your attention back to the point of time where you say that you were fleeing with your wife and son but you were shot and you returned.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber if you were eventually captured.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber the date of your capture.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The 12th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's start again. Tell the Trial Chamber the date of your capture. You said that you -- the attack took place on --

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The 7th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. And that's the 7th of January?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when were you captured, how many days after the attack were you captured?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Five days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the 12th of January?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do in between the date of the attack and your capture?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was hiding around the village. I would go out in the evenings to get warm on the ashes of the houses that had been burned. I hid and that's how I stayed there for five days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had been shot in your lower leg, in your calf, I believe?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to still walk, get around, with that wound?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I walked slowly. I bandaged it with some old rags, and I used a stick.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you eat?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On the 7th of January, they stole the dried meat from -- the cured meat I had. But I still had some pieces of bacon left. For five days I ate what little food I could scavenge. I would put some potatoes in the fire and bake them, and I had a bit of bacon to eat with those potatoes. And that's what I had to eat for those five days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were hiding around the village. Which village are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Zonjici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to go down to where your house had been?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What remained?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Nothing. On Friday fire was set to it. I went out under cover of night, so as not to be seen or I would have been killed. But there was nothing left. I had more than one house there but nothing was left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many houses did you have on your property?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they both burnt?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your barns, were they burnt?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your neighbours' --

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me finish.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The houses and barns of your neighbours in Zonjici, were they also destroyed in a similar fashion?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you hiding during the day?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was hiding in a hollow tree. I collected embers from the fires and that's where I hid during the day. In the evening I went to the burnt houses to get warm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those days prior to your capture, did you see any armed men?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would see them walking around the villages. Whoever had livestock, that was driven away, and they were walking around looking for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnicity of the armed men that you saw?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It's what we used to call Muslims. Now I suppose they're Bosniaks. Everybody had fled after Christmas and those who hadn't fled had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber why you say the men you saw who were armed were Muslims or Bosniaks. What makes you say that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Nobody else came to the village after it was burnt down, only them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear them speaking? Did you ever get close enough to them to hear them speaking?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were these armed men dressed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They were wearing different-coloured clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what sort of clothes?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Normal suits like mine. They were not wearing camouflage uniforms. It was civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to these armed men that you've told us were walking around, did you see any other people in company with the armed men?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any items being removed from houses?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It was done by the people who went to the villages to collect things, and they were escorted by soldiers with weapons. I was hiding in a hollow tree and I could see them taking my things away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you about your property and Zonjici in a moment, but I'm really more interested at this stage in Kravica and Siljkovici and Opravdici. Did you see any personal possessions being taken away in Opravdici, Kravica, and Siljkovici?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Siljkovici's further off. I was not able to see that. As for the rest I was able to see -- not Opravdici I was able to see as much as in Zonjici. I hid near Zonjici in places where I could not be seen, because if they'd seen me they would have killed me. Therefore I was able to see something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you -- let me rephrase that. In Opravdici did you see anyone taking possessions away from the houses?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that people were taking possessions away from the houses in Opravdici, were they in company with armed men?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Opravdici when the people were taking things away from the houses in company with armed men, what sort of things were they taking away?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Whatever they could lay their hands on, mostly food and livestock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'll ask you about your property in particular. You've said earlier in your testimony that you owned livestock including cattle. After the attack what happened to your cattle?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On the morning of the attack when my wife, my child, and I left, they left towards Popovici and towards the Drina to cross over into Serbia because you could still pass through. The road had not been blocked yet. Once I returned I did not dare go back home directly, so I went back to the woods and hid in a hollow tree trunk. In the evening when I came my house had been burned and my livestock was gone; it had been driven off. You could see the trail leading towards Kravica, the livestock and the cows. I had three pigs about 100 kilogrammes each. They were gone. And when I opened the pigsty the next morning, I found that one of the pigs had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shot?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, shot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't actually see your cattle being taken, you deduce that they were taken because you saw the tracks in the snow. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go now to your capture. You said that was the 12th of January. It was -- what day of the week was that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who captured you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When I left the shelter in which I was hiding, a hollow tree trunk, I came to my village, to Zonjici, and I was looking at Kravica. From the direction of Bacici I saw something like a bullet being fired and someone said "Halt." There were seven armed soldiers. I put my arms up in the air and they drove us on to Kravica and then from Kravica to Lolici. From Lolici the van drove over Tursunovic was in the combi and he was escorted by Naser Oric. They took me as far as the Zesta crossroads. From there they walked and I walked with them until past Potocarska Rijeka where we got into a car again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm going to ask you about those matters first -- later, but I want some more detail. You say you were captured by seven armed soldiers. Do you know the ethnicity of those armed soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Probably they were Bosniak when they captured me and drove me away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- do you now have any memory of what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Different kinds of clothes but civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of them armed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were captured near Zonjici?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From there, did you walk to Kravica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from Kravica to Lolici, how did you travel?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We walked. They made me walk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You walked to Kravica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But from Kravica to Lolici, how did you go?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I walked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about Kravica. Was this the first time you actually went into the village of Kravica since the 7th of January?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you have an opportunity to look around and see what the place looked like?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see any damage to the buildings in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber the extent of damage and what sort of damage you could see.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I saw houses burned and buildings. These are things that I saw in passing, but I couldn't see the exact extent. I'd say roughly about 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were some of the houses still smoking?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see people taking things?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of things?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was not able to see exactly what people were carrying in their sacks, but they were picking things up, whatever they could find. Some were taking away roof tiles and construction materials, things from houses, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there armed men in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. From Kravica you continued your walk to Lolici?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how far is that, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think the distance is about 3, 3 and a half kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to walk -- obviously you were able to walk. Let me --

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I did try to walk as fast as I could. They made me walk fast but I couldn't. They beat me and they slapped me, so I had no choice but to keep on walking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened when you arrived in Lolici?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in Lolici, when we arrived at the crossroads there, a van came from the direction of Konjevic Polje. In the van there was Tursunovic, Zulfo, 14 of his escorts, and Mr. Naser Oric. He came out and then about 50 or 100 people came over from Lolici and they kept saying, "Let's look at this Chetnik." And Zulfo said, "Don't touch him, he's going to Srebrenica with us." So they put me back in the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's slow down. How big was this van?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The van was the regular kind. A passenger van. I would say it had up to 20 seats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were the men who were in it armed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they uniformed or in ordinary civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Three were in white camouflage and the rest were in -- wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were taken from the -- in the van to where?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: To the Zesta [phoen] crossroads and Lolici. They couldn't cross the hill. We walked until Potocarska Rijeka. I don't know the name of the village, it's past Jaglici and then again we ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the Zesta crossroad fairly close to Zesta?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the trip take from Lolici to the Zesta crossroad?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It did take a while. The vehicle was not very good and I think it took about one hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the Zesta crossroad where did you walk to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We used a detour through Zesta to reach Jaglici and then Jaglici and from there on to Potocarska Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was walking?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Walking, yes, across the hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you leave the van?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At the Zesta crossroad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the walk from the Zesta crossroad to Potocari take?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Over two hours, probably. I didn't have a watch on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from Potocari to Srebrenica, how did you make your way there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We arrived at Potocarska Rijeka. I'm not sure of the name of the that village is. There were two cars there. We got into these two cars and were then taken to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did that take?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Maybe one and a half hours. From Potocarska Rijeka to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the men who were -- let me rephrase that. The men who were in the van when you first saw them, did they remain with you to the Zesta crossroad to Potocari and to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that period of time, including the two-hour walk across the hills or thereabouts, did you have an opportunity to look at them, hear them talk, watch them walk, converse amongst themselves, see their faces, see the backs of their heads, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that two of the men in the van, you've mentioned their names, Zulfo Tursunovic and Naser Oric. What makes you say that one of the men in the van was Zulfo Tursunovic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I met Zulfo Tursunovic in Srebrenica because he would come to see us in prison every day and his soldiers called him "Mr. Zulfo."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that, him being addressed as Mr. Zulfo, in the van, during the walk, or in the cars on the way to Srebrenica? Did you hear?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I also heard that in Lolici when those other people came to have a look at the Chetnik. He said, "Don't touch him. We'll yet be needing him." And they said, "Thank you very much, Mr. Zulfo." So I took notice of that and I heard it a number of times on the way to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Mr. Zulfo look like? Can you describe him to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zulfo was a tall man, elderly; a green beret; a short, clipped moustache. And he was carrying an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever seen him or laid eyes on him prior to this day?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second man you said that you -- was on the bus who you named was Naser Oric. Why do you see that he was on the bus?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I saw him take his seat behind the driver. He was seated just behind the driver in the van.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, maybe you saw him. But why do you say it was Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I saw as we were travelling the soldiers were getting out of the way saying, "Naser Oric is passing through." Because the road is narrow through the woods and fields and the soldiers were getting out of the way left and right saying, "Let Naser Oric pass."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What did he look like?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Naser Oric had green clothes on and a weapon called Scorpio. It's a large weapon and I saw other people talking among themselves saying, "Oh, it's a Scorpio." So that's the sort of weapon he had, and green clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have -- your evidence has been that all of these men including Mr. Oric and Tursunovic walked across to Potocari. Was Mr. Oric armed during that walk?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he do anything with his gun that you remember?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: A pistol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What did he do with the pistol that you remember?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He just kept this pistol. It was tucked into his belt and then he would spin it around his finger. He didn't use it, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not suggested he did. But you remember this spinning action with the pistol?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. He held it like that on the way down to Drljevo [phoen]. He was spinning it around his finger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the man that you say was Naser Oric ever issue any orders or commands that you heard - I'm talking about what you heard now - at any time in the vans or in the walk across the hills to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours just bear with me for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The trip from Potocari to Srebrenica, I think you said it required two cars. Do I understand you that the soldiers who had accompanied you across the mountain or the hills got into those two cars with you and then drove together to Srebrenica? Is my understanding correct or not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which car were you in or on?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Those were TAM trucks, rather one was a TAM truck and the other was a van, but that was 11 years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that a lot's happened since then and I'm not asking for every single detail, only what you can recall. First of all, what vehicle did you travel on, the TAM, the TAM truck, or the other van?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: A TAM truck that was open and there were three men on it together with me who had camouflage uniforms on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned two of the men who accompanied you as being Zulfo Tursunovic and Naser Oric. Were they in the TAM truck or in the other vehicle?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They were in the van.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did both vehicles travel together close to each other in convoy to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you been to Srebrenica before?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, about two or three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you -- is it the case that you knew Srebrenica but not that well?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We were taken from Potocarska Rijeka to Srebrenica. In Srebrenica they stopped somewhere and two of those three wearing camouflage uniform grabbed me by the arm and took me to the police station. At the police station there's a duty room, 2 by 2 metres. They left me in that room. I saw Kostadin Popovic and Mica Milovanovic there, and a man named Drago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that to remain your cell there for some time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were placed into custody by the armed -- some of the armed men?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who had escorted you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to the actual prison now, if Your Honours please. MR. DI FAZIO: Would that be an appropriate time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's perfect with us. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Nikolic, I want to ask you about your first night in prison. This was in the SUP building in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anyone else in the cell with you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Kostadin Popovic, Mico Milovanovic, and an old man called Drago from Zesta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What constitutes an old man sometimes changes. Now, was he a very old man? In his 60s? Can you give us any idea?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Over 80, over 80.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So he was 80 years young. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him at the time as Drago or did you later find out that that had been his name?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I learned that in the morning when he died. The others knew him, Kostadin and Mico because he had arrived five days before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about Kostadin Popovic, did he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Kojo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other gentleman Mico Milovanovic, did he have a nickname or was he known as Mico?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know either Kostadin or Mico from before or was that the first time you met those men?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I knew Kostadin but not Mico.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old were Kostadin and Mico approximately?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Kostadin was born in 1947. As for Mico, I don't know, but he was younger. He was between 35 and 40.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spent some time in the cells with Mico and Kostadin. Can you recall at all what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Kostadin and Mico, I remember well, were wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have blood on them when you first laid eyes on them?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would object to that question. If he could just ask them to the described rather than suggesting that they were already in some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection sustained. Objection sustained . Mr. Di Fazio, please. You know better. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Describe the appearance of these men, Kostadin, Mico, and Drago.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When I arrived on the 12th in the evening, on the following day, the 13th, in the morning Drago died. They had blood on their faces. They hadn't watched their faces. But I didn't see the wounds or the bandages because they had arrived in the prison five days before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything on their clothes? Were their clothes clean or dirty?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Dirty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With what?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they had blood on their faces, blood on their clothes, and one of them died in the night?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's unclear to me whether they're all supposed to have blood on them. Mr. Di Fazio is merging them all together. Perhaps we should deal with them one by one. Otherwise the suggestion is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think there was one question and if the witness wanted or needed to distinguish between one and the other, he would have distinguished. So I think when he gave the answer that he did he meant both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Or the three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But particularly, it's just the way that Mr. Di Fazio put the question, it suggests the person who died died because of something to do with the blood on him and that's a matter which -- which we need to be clear about and not vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's a conclusion that will be drawn later on based on the facts, not on what they were wearing, or whether what they were wearing was soiled or not. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll clarify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described the men in the cells a having blood on their faces and blood on their clothes. Did they apply to all three men?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Drago was alive when you arrived, but dead in the morning. Is that the scenario?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Drago was alive when I arrived on the 12th and during the night he died in the 13th, on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did-- apart from the blood on his face did he have any apparent wounds that you could see?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of wounds? Where were they located?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On his face. I couldn't see under his clothes, but on his face. Just as I did. You could see every wound on the face and that's where the blood came from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there cuts on his face?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were his eyes swollen?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened with his body?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the morning two men took Drago out on a stretcher and took him away from me and Mico and Kojo. I don't know where they took him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this stage had you been beaten? I'm talking about the point of time where -- the point morning when Drago was taken away. Had you yet at that point in time being subjected to any beating?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the police station, where we were locked up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of beating had you suffered?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Through the bars, the bars were far apart and you can see the cuts here. You can still see them on my face. They would push their arms through the bars. It was night so you couldn't see very well, but here you can see all the scars on my face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about what happened to you in your time in custody and I'll get to more details later. But just understand this: I'm only talking about when you first arrived, when you first arrived at Srebrenica, that first night when you walked in and saw Drago and Mico and Kojo, now, that first night, were you beaten or not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to -- sorry. Let me withdraw that. The following day, what date was that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The following day was the 13th. It was Wednesday. I remember very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain in your cell throughout that day?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the morning when it got light, in the morning of the 13th, a man arrived and he said, "Who arrived last night?" I said I had. He took me out and took me upstairs at the police station. There was a man sitting there and there was a pistol and a knife there on the table. And the man who had brought me in went away and the two of us were in the office. He asked me what a knife was used for and I was very frightened. And I said, "It can be used for anything." And he said to me, "The purpose of this knife is to slaughter, to cut throats." He spoke quite a lot. I didn't dare say anything. He asked what salt was used for. And I said, "Well, to put in food," and, or -- and he would say to me, "It's for killing." And then this other man took me back -- oh, yes, he asked me what I had at home, how much. He asked me about my family members. I said I had a wife and two sons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown P47, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have an objection to P47, and it's a fairly -- it's fairly lengthy to set out precisely what we object to, so I don't know whether we should deal with that now before the witness is shown the document or afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, if he is being shown the document now and you have an objection, I think we need to hear what the objection is about and this must not be done in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed, indeed, Your Honour, that's my concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what I suggest is that Madam Usher will escort the witness out, take him to his room and offer him a coffee while we deal with this. How long do you think this matter will require?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Probably only ten minutes, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, all right. Let's have the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We'll deal with this matter. Was the Prosecution given advance notice that you would be questioning -- objecting to P47?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We've always objected to this document, as indeed all documents from that source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I didn't specifically inform the Prosecution that I was going to stand up at this moment and make objections in this format, but we've always objected to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Well, the objections we have to this document need also be seen in relation to another document which the Prosecution has alerted us they may be intending to use. But I'll start just with this document alone. And firstly, it's a handwritten piece of paper with an illegible signature, an illegible seal, and we say it could have been written at any time by anybody, firstly. Secondly, the source, we say, is questionable. It's the Sokolac collection, it's from the Sokolac collection, and as we have seen to a certain extent with Ms. Manas and as we will see some more when she comes back, we have very strong, reasoned objections to documents from that source. Thirdly, there are a number of highly suspect features about this document. It refers to a high military court, which never existed as far as we know. The handwriting isn't consistent as some bits in capitals, some bits which appear to be in different handwriting. We don't know who signed it. Fourthly, there's at least one sentence which is wrongly translated. In English we have: "He is still evasive, continue the stepped-up treatment." We've looked at that line in Bosnian and tried to decipher and tried translate it and we certainly don't accept that that's a correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's according to you the correct translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, it's very difficult to read a couple of the words. What we could do is put it on the ELMO and see if the interpreters can help us with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can always put this on the ELMO now. This is the line solitary line that there is just below the date 22/01/1993. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, I know. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours wish you could look at it on Sanction, I'm told, if that's more convenient for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can certainly look at it on Sanction, but the important thing is we must zoom in. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's computer evidence. That's in English. We want it in the original. That's it. And now it's that line just below -- beneath the date 22/01/1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think the interpreters -- okay. I don't know if the interpreters are able to read it, first of all, just in the original.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's very difficult, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's very difficult they tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, can we enlarge it further? Can it be enlarged any further? MR. DI FAZIO: Apparently not. I think it will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think if we put it on the ELMO, I think it stands a chance of being enlarged better. Let's try. And we can take it -- we can take it, word or in parts. First -- yeah. And we move it to the left. Does it help you any further?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can try, Your Honour. "He is still" --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... in Bosnian, I think, just so we know what -- if -- if -- could the interpreters read what the words are in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If the interpreters can read it also in Bosnian first or B/C/S, Serb.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot be absolutely sure, Your Honour, but I think it might be [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which would translate into what?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, we have not heard the interpretation of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could I ask the interpreters to repeat the words -- I think you have to switch on to the English, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Could I kindly ask you to repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which would translate into what in English?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "He is still evading, continue with a strengthened regime."
