utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's different from the English translation. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm happy with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So that's one of the objections, anyway, I don't wish to dwell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Of course. But certainly as you see how important it is that this is not discussed in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, Your Honour. Now, as far as this document is concerned, my fifth objection relates to another document which, as I said, the Prosecution intends to, or has told us they intend to use today, and that's with the ERN 02075708. We're going to pass out copies of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The reason I say it has to be seen in relation to that document is because this document says at the bottom: "Opinion written on the 1st of February, 1993." And then we have another document which appears or purports to be a writing-up of the notes of interrogation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This we don't have. I don't think we have this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if we look at this document, this is one of the documents where we've challenged the authenticity of it and Your Honours will see why. There are two versions of this document which we've received, one with the ERN 02075708, and one with the ERN 02075791. And if Your Honours have both those documents -- do you have them both?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You'll see that the body of the document is clearly the same -- in fact, you can see the corrections to the word halfway down [B/C/S spoken]. There's a typing correction. There's another one in the next line [B/C/S spoken]. We can see that that's clearly the same document. But then we have, down the bottom, the signature is different, the stamp moved into the middle of the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The writing at the top of the page, the 7 and the 30 -- 01 are different. But that aside, what's much more important is one of the documents simply says in handwritten at the bottom "razminjin" [phoen], exchanged. And that's the one that the Prosecution is planning to use with this witness. But the other copy which was disclosed to us in the C binder of supporting materials says: "Exchanged 7th of February, 1993," if you see the English translation of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's terribly important to us because the witness's evidence, at least according to his 2000 statement to the investigators, is that he was exchanged on the 26th of February, 1993. So this document saying he was exchanged on the 7th of February, 1993, contradicts his evidence, the evidence we expect he will be giving, therefore exculpatory under Rule 68 material. But aside from that, it shows either that the witness was exchanged much earlier than he says or there is something fraudulent about this document because it contains that false information. And as I said, this document has to be seen in relation to P47 because P47 says that the opinion was written on the 1st of February, whereas this document shows the opinion was written on the 30th of January, 1993. So there's yet another inconsistency. And then moving beyond that, this document is purportedly signed by Hamid Salihovic. And we have -- we and the Prosecution have documents, we've been -- disclosed documents by the Prosecution showing that Hamid Salihovic resigned on the 21st of December, 1992, and we have copies of that document to hand up. That has been disclosed by the Prosecution in the F binder. The ERN for that document is 03577310. If I could just draw Your Honours' attention to the fist -- to the date, first of all. Then, "Decision to leave the Srebrenica OS staff due to the thankless position and conditions in which we find ourselves in the overall activities, we the undersigned members of the Srebrenica OS staff hereby submit our resignations from the Srebrenica OS staff." And then one goes to the end, and number one, we see Hamid Salihovic signed that. And then that's then confirmed by a witness who will be testifying against Naser Oric, Dr. Nedret Mujkanovic who in his statement to the ICTY of the 4th of June, 2004, which we also have copies of, confirmed that Mr. Salihovic resigned that and he was never replaced. If the usher could assist with that. So in this statement, Nedret Mujkanovic, dated 4th of June 2004. We have the extracts from paragraphs three, five, and six, and he says: "I've been shown an original document bearing ERN 01839515 to 01839516," now, that's the resignation letter. And in fact the copy we handed up has been signed by Mr. Mujkanovic. "I can confirm the contents of this document. These persons did submit their resignations. All the reasons mentioned in this document for the resignation of the members of the OS staff Srebrenica are quite genuine." And paragraph 5: "Apart from Abdul Muhic, rest of the members of OS Srebrenica staff like Hamid Salihovic et cetera did resign from their positions. As far as I know their positions were never filled up. These resignations did materialise." Paragraph 6: "Nobody was appointed to replace Hamid Salihovic as the head of security and intelligence." And a bit further down: "Mr. Salihovic went to Potocari and was not active anymore." So we have Mr. Salihovic resigning on the 21st of December, 1992, going to Potocari, not having any further activities, the position is not being filled up. And then this document, which we've already pointed out some speeches signed by Hamid Salihovic on the 30th of January, 1993. So -- so for those reasons, we absolutely don't accept either P47 or this other document, 02075708.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But then, Mr. Jones, are you suggesting that the signature of Hamid Salihovic as it appears on both documents, that is 5708 and 5791 is forged?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Those are the submissions I wish to make, Your Honour, unless I can assist you further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours -- if Your Honours please, all of the matters raised by Mr. Jones go to the weight that you should attach to this document, each and every matter. The document was initially admitted into -- has been admitted into evidence and I must be in a position to be able to use it and utilise it with witnesses as they come along. The weight that you later give to this document is a matter for you which you will make in the light of can what this witness said about it and everything that Mr. Jones has raised. And later of course we can -- there might be other evidence that touches upon the authenticity or lack of authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: But that's nothing that should prevent me now from showing to the witness and extracting whatever evidence I can get on it. So in terms of evidence, I simply say, well, whatever -- all Mr. Jones has said simply doesn't mean I can't show it to him. As far as there being two copies is concerned, I think that the Defence was quite right to point it out and unfortunately I don't have copies of the second document made. I realise that I should produce both copies to the witness. I've only got copies of one of them -- one of the versions of this document. So if you would permit me, I would like to arrange for copies to be made of that so I can ensure that any -- all of the parties and the Court have the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have both.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's P69, actually, the other one. 02075791 is P69. And the other document, 02075708, the Prosecution should have because they planned to use it today. MR. DI FAZIO: That solves -- I'm grateful to Mr. Jones. I should have known that, and that solves the problem. But -- so my submission is: I can show it to the witness and everything raised is a matter of authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime -- MR. DI FAZIO: As far as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, go ahead, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: All I really wanted to do with this witness is touch upon matters of esoteric knowledge in this document. There's things in here that only he -- that's the evidence I wanted to extract from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. In the meantime let's do things in an orderly manner. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, in the course of your submissions, you made reference to three -- basically four documents. Are you tendering them now? Because I think it's the case of tendering them now and then if need be we'll come back to them at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. We'll tender those which aren't exhibits already. So that would go for the extract from the statement of Dr. Nedret Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go through this carefully. Now, document with ERN number 02075708 will become Defence Exhibit D113.1. 113.1 -- 114? 114.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarity, obviously we're not putting that forward as an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. Obviously you don't even need to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Document with ERN number 02075791 will become Defence Exhibit D114.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's the one which is already P69.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that -- don't worry. I mean, it -- I'm attaching them together so that when later on --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When the submissions are seen together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the English translation which is L0099248, I think, and 249 will be the corresponding translation of D114.2. So one would be A and the other one would be B, I suppose. Which one are we using for the English? E? E. So the English translation would be E, D114.2E. The statement of Nedret Mujkanovic which has ERN number 03577298. 298 and 299 will become D115. And the letter of resignation of the individuals amongst who supposedly is Hamid Salihovic with ERN number 03577310 to 311 will become D116.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I might just briefly in reply to my learned friend say that obviously there are -- these are matters which go to the weight of the document, but to show it to the witness and have him possibly confirm personal details is -- firstly, would wrongly, possibly, create the impression that the document has a value which it doesn't have. And secondly would be pointless because those details can be elicited from the witness simply by asking him who his wife is, who his parents are, who his children are, and any of the other details which the Prosecution might wish to submit or confirm by the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you intend to show him the document -- MR. DI FAZIO: I'm happy to adopt the second course of action. But in order for -- if I do that, I would ask that the Trial Chamber look at the document while that particular portion of evidence is being elicited so you can evaluate it. I'm happy not to show -- the point that Mr. Jones makes is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. I think we can go along with it. MR. DI FAZIO: Deal with it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, certainly. Certainly So are we ready with this argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we will need to take -- give a ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So our ruling is -- along the line of consistency with what we said in the beginning of this trial that matters of authenticity and probative value and weight that will be given to the document is an exercise that will be carried out in the end, having heard all the evidence. We might even have Mr. Hamid Salihovic come here and say, "No, that's not forged. That's my signature." Or come here and say, "That's not my signature."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wonder while I'm on my feet. We have an objection to another document which might subsequently be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's decide this. The document will be made use of. Of course, we've taken note of all your objections, and at the end we will decide what weight to give this document, if at all. Because, I mean, we might agree completely with you that -- and give your client the benefit of the doubt. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, I'm obliged, Your Honour. I just mention it now that there is another document which we will be contesting if the Prosecution seeks to use it. I don't know if while the witness is out of the room it's worth referring to that or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you think or you have an indication that this document is going to be used today, yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, it would seem a more sufficient course. Well, there's a hospital discharge certificate, which I understand the Prosecution sin tending to use with this witness. If Your Honours will give me one moment just to have that in front of me. And actually if the usher could pass up copies, please. And the English translation bears the ERN 00366743. And if one sees the second page of that document at the bottom signed with the name -- Ljubisav Gavric is the bottom. But it says: "N.b., officially authorised by the undersigned. The discharge certificate could not be reproduced." And on the front page it says it is a copy. In fact, as we understand it, this is a re-typing of a document. It's not actually the original. It's not even the copy of an original. It's as if I were to take a document being tendered in this case, take it home with me, type it up, and come back with that document, and put that as -- forward as evidence. We say it's unreliable. It fails the best evidence rule if one wants to use that term which is used in Your Honours' order on -- order concerning guidelines on evidence in the conduct of parties during trial proceedings. We say that, you know, a copy is one thing but a document that has been re-typed and where it's clear from the face of the document that it's not -- it's not the actual certificate. The discharge certificate could not be reproduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's ask for some help here from the interpreters. What's the correct translation of "prepis" [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what do the boards [B/C/S spoken] mean?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Letter of discharge from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the meaning of [B/C/S spoken]?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Letter of discharge again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, but the two mean the same thing, but they are not the same, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: These are both copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but every one -- every document is a copy. In other words, basically what --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This I understand is really the words at the end: "The discharge certificate could not be reproduced. " I understand that to mean this isn't even a photocopy of the discharge certificate. If it could be produced it could be photocopied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know what to tell you, Mr. Jones, but again --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Also the date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I -- there are, I suppose, a hundred and one reasons which you can think of to complain against this document, whether it's the first format, and I would join you there because most of it you can't even read, at least the photocopy that we have. And I agree with you that where you have copy, it's -- basically it's not a copy. But the first one is also a copy. And the words sometimes are not exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Because the original -- if this were a photocopy of an original document it wouldn't have the words "copy" actually typed on it and it wouldn't have the "n.b." typed on the end. So this is where it's fundamentally different from a photocopy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But is there any indication -- because that -- this is forged or this is false? Because let's take the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's really this, Your Honour, it says: "Hospital discharge certificate." And then at the end it says, "the discharge certificate could not be reproduced."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but, again, in the first of these two documents just before -- on top of the signature, the words that I can see there are not the same as the words in the nota bene part of the second document where you see [B/C/S spoken]. If you read the previous document, it doesn't say that. It says: [B/C/S spoken]. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As far as that's concerned, Your Honour, it may be that this is a retranslation back into Bosnian -- or B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what to tell you, Mr. Jones, but I wouldn't waste time on this. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You have my submissions, Your Honour. There is one other matter which is this document refers to the witness being hospitalised from the 1st of March, 1993. We understand his evidence will be that he was hospitalised from the 26th of February, so -- and our indication that there's something, we say, fishy about this document. But my submissions are on the record and we can leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, I think we are not tendering this document for the time being. We are just leaving it here. If it's made use of, I think we have taken note of your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It was really to get them on record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I agree, and appreciate the attention you are giving to the documents because that is very much helpful. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. I don't think you need to answer. So I think we'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's bring in the witness and continue, please. MR. DI FAZIO: I might just tell you that I'll elicit evidence from this witness about what happened to him post his exchange. If I'm satisfied with that, I won't even use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: Now, can I ask now that Your Honours have the documents that we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P47. MR. DI FAZIO: P47 And I think now that you can have D114.1 and .2 so you have both of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, they are here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I want to ask you some questions about the 13th of January. You said that you had an encounter with a man and you described the knife and the salt. And you also said in evidence that you provided a number of personal details to him. I just want to ask you some -- forget about that encounter. I just want to ask you some personal details. What's your wife's maiden name?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Marija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's her first name. Her maiden name, her surname before he married you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is she from?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Bratinski [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever been to a place called Gornji Mratinci?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year was your son Goran born?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992 or -- and early --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In 1992 where was your son working, Goran I mean?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He worked for Elektroserbija [phoen] in Belgrade. He was an electrical engineer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what year was your son Zoran born?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier today you testified that he had been in hospital. Where -- did he have an injury?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What part of his body was injured?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: His leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to elementary school?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You missed the location of the hospital, Mr. ... MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, I'm sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said earlier today that your son had been in hospital. Where was the hospital that he had been in? I'm talking about Zoran.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In Serbia, Loznica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you complete elementary school or do some grades at elementary school?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Elementary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. How many grades --

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you do your military -- did you do military service?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In Milana [phoen], eleven months and six in Skopje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Between 1964 and 1967, the 13th of September, 1964, I left [as interpreted]. And in 1967, I left the military. I had served for 17 months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you do -- did you acquire any specialities when you were performing your military service?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Signals, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier today that you had troubles with a hernia in 1992. Did you have any other health problems in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of problems?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My heart wasn't really working properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you own television sets in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember how many TVs you had in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have wheat stored at your farm?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have sheep, cattle, pigs, chickens?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man named Miso Eric?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Heard of, but I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know his wife's name?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He had died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know his wife's name?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I must have heard it but I can't remember it properly. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Apart from the salt and the knife being present during the interview on the 13th of January, were you asked a lot -- a number of personal questions by your interrogator, whoever it was?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just answer me yes or no: In the weeks that followed the 13th of January, were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that frequently or -- can you give the Trial Chamber any idea of how often?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Whenever those people came to look at the Chetniks they beat us, but there were two of them who came regularly to beat us two or three times. They wore black caps or balaclavas with slits for the eyes. And those were the two persons who beat us the most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall any other occasion similar to the one that you've described on the 13th of January when you were asked questions by anyone, another interrogation of sorts? Did that ever happen again if you can recall? If you can't recall, that's fine. But if you can, tell us.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to ask you about the beatings and in order to fix things in your mind about the time period I'm asking you about, firstly I'll ask you this: Was there ever an occasion in January when more people were brought into or brought into custody?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically what the date was, the 15th or the 16th when Skelani was attacked and four other men were brought in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask you about that later. So now I'm going to ask you questions about the period of time between the 12th when you were captured and the 16th when these people from Skelani came. Now, in that time, as I understand your evidence, you were in custody with Kojo and with Mico. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during that period of time were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the other two then in your cell, Mico and Kojo, beaten?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall who it was that beat you and the other men?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know why they beat us, but they kept coming all the time. Probably on someone's orders or maybe of their own free will. I really don't know the reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But me question is really this: How often did it happen? Was it every day? Every second or third day? Can you give the Trial Chamber an idea of the frequency. And remember, I'm just talking about that first period of time when you were in custody, that -- the period of time between your capture and the people from Skelani --

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Daily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it the case that only --

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They beat us on a daily basis, day and night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and the other two men in the cell?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were instruments used?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, probably because when they got through the bars you realised later it was a prison a room inside the police station, it was only 2 by 2, so if you put a stick through the bars you could beat someone who was inside the room and I still have scars by being struck by those sticks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your assailants ever open the cell doors and come in and beat you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you all right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you ever kicked?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, and we were no longer able to stand up. So we sat next to the wall and that's when they kicked us. We had been starved and we were already worn out by the beatings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You've mentioned the name of Mr. Zulfo Tursunovic. In the initial part of your incarceration - again I'm talking about the period of time between your capture and the arrival of the men -- of the other prisoners from Skelani around mid-January - during that period, that short period of time, did you ever see him?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, he came to the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall -- sorry. Did you actually see him, see him for yourself?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. I saw him inside the cell but not outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you've actually laid eyes on him?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. In the cell, yes, we were able to see him but not outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. What did he say, if anything?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Nothing. He would come. He saw us covered in blood. He would always ask, "What's happened to you?" We were not able to say anything who beat us. We just shrugged our shoulders and kept silent. We knew as soon as he left the same men were there to beat us, therefore we just kept silent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the men were being beaten, and yourself included, were they screaming?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Milosava Nikolic, the women who were there, 14 women and four children in the adjacent room, they could hear us scream and moan but it was just no use that they did. It was no help. There were women there who were also detained who could hear us cry out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's be clear about this for the Trial Chamber, now. Now, we're talking about the SUP building here, the SUP building, were there women incarcerated in the SUP building? Think carefully about the question.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there -- were you later moved from the SUP building and taken elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When they took us from the police station, they took us to the centre between the court and the municipality. There's a passage on the upper side and there is a cell there, a prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that where the women were imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now, I'll take you back to the SUP building. That's where I'm -- what I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please speak into the microphone. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm terribly sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the second time, Mr. Di Fazio. The third time we will fall down very heavily on you. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I apologise. I'll raise my voice as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is Monday, don't worry. You don't need to worry. It's the -- Monday at noon, that's what you hear. So it's a rehearsal. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask you now of the arrival of the prisoners from Skelani. You say that they arrived around the 15th or the 16th of January, 1993. Is that when you were transferred?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all three of the men who were in the SUP building transferred to this other location that you've already told us about?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you placed in a cell or room at this building near the municipal building in company with other male prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about who was in custody -- I want to ask you about who was in custody in this second prison that you've told us about. Was Kojo there or Kostadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mico Milanovic there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mico Milovanovic, Kostadin, Ilija, from Skelani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You did what I wanted you to do. As you're going through the names tell us where they're from, if you recall. Okay? So, you've told us Kostadin. You've told us Ilija from Skelani. Continue.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Jakov Kalabaca from Siljkovici; Dragan Kasaba, Vlasenica; Mico Milovanovic, Sase; Srebrenica. There was some elderly people, Mico from Kasaba. Jakov Kalabaca from Vlasenica; and there were some elderly men from Skelani. There were over 80 and I don't know their names. [As interpreted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I need to suspend the sitting for just two minutes. We'll be back in two minutes. MR. DI FAZIO: Certainly, Your Honours. --- Break taken at 12.04 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies to Mr. Di Fazio for interrupting you like this, but -- MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- let's proceed. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period of time in which you were incarcerated did you ever meet a woman named Andza?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was she incarcerated?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, all of these names you've mentioned, did they all arrive at the same time from Skelani or did they -- did some of them arrive from Skelani and others arrive later from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They didn't all arrive at the same time. Some were in Pobudje three of them, in Dandje [phoen]. They arrived in Srebrenica in early February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which ones were the ones that came in early February?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Jakov, Mico, Dragan, and Andza. Andza was in the women's prison and those three were with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So Jakov from Kalabaca, Dragan from Kosarava [phoen], and Mico from Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that a different Mico from Mico Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: There were two men called Mico. These were just their nicknames. I didn't know their full names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, I understand. All right. Now though -- they -- they arrived in February, but now turn your mind back to mid-January and tell us which ones arrived from Skelani. We're not talking about Andza, Jakov, Dragan, or Mico, but which ones came in from Skelani?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Ilija and the man who died with Kostadin. I didn't know his name. And two who were exchanged when the women were exchanged on the 6th of February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man who died with Kostadin, was he -- what age was he approximately?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He was over 65, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of a hamlet called Rasica Gaj?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the old man who was over 65 with -- who died, do you know where he was from?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He came from Skelani, but what the name of the hamlet was I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any male prisoner in the cells with you who was handicapped?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: From Kalabaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, not Kalabaca, Rogaci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Branko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember the surname?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I used to know it but now it escapes me. Sekulic, Branko. Sekulic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. And what was his handicap?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He was wounded somewhere on Rogaci through the leg he couldn't get up or walk about. He was down there in the hospital and then one evening they brought him to us in the prison and he also had a bad arm. He didn't have any fingers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the lack of fingers, did you understand that to be from some sort of industrial accident before the war?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there anyone in custody with you who was paralyzed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, Stanoje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did Stanoje come from? Was he one of the men who came in from Skelani or was he brought in at some later point?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He was brought in with the other three from Skelani who were born in Skelani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you ever provided with any information as to where Andza; Jakov from Kalabaca; Dragan from Kasaba; and Mico from Kasaba had been prior to their being taken to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. They told us when they arrived from Srebrenica where they had been in prison and how long in Pobudje. For seven months they were locked up in a stable there. And then in early February, I don't know the date, they were brought to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You were eventually -- I don't think this is in dispute. You were eventually exchanged on the 27th of February or thereabouts. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to that were a number of women exchanged?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall approximately when the women were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of February, Saturday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the male prisoners who were being held with you exchanged at the same time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Stanoje and an elderly man whose name I don't know, but I've mentioned him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to ask you now about the period of time from when you first arrived in this second prison behind the municipality and the exchange of the women on about the 6th of February. Okay. So that period of time from about mid-January to the exchange. Are you clear about that? That's what I'm going to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that period of time were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see other men in the cell with you also beaten?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've described the use of instruments --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry. I wasn't clear where or when that happened. I would be grateful if for this part of the witness's testimony Mr. Di Fazio could abstain from leading as much as possible. MR. DI FAZIO: I withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he mentioned the use of sticks before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In the SUP building. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the question is perfectly legitimate if I read you well. You've mentioned the use of sticks when you were in the SUP building. Now that you've been transferred to another place, the prison, were sticks used as well or was it different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was any other instrument used apart from sticks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever they had. If they were carrying a rifle, they would hit us with the rifle butt and they would hit us all over, anywhere, in the stomach. I was beaten all the time. They punched me with their fists. I still have a loose tooth. When Kostadin Popovic died on the 6th in the night he was beaten three times and this other man, when he was exhumed you can see that his head was smashed up. They beat him three times on that night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about the night of the 6th in a bit more detail but I'm just you more general questions now in the period of time between mid-January up until that very night. Okay? Now, in that period of time did you have blood on you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the other men have blood on them and on their clothing?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber of the frequency of beatings between mid-January and the 6th of February. How often did it happen?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Every day. You couldn't count the number of times. Whenever anyone came by. They beat us on a regular basis, two, three. I can't remember everything that happened 10 or 11 years later, but I remember a lot because my head was injured. I get lost sometimes. I was beaten every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever cut?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, here. I can't recall the date when the guard opened the door of our cell and a man came in. He had a big beard. His sleeves were rolled up. He grabbed me and he put his knife here. And the ones who were standing guard in front of the door, they said, "Don't cut his throat, we will be punished by Mr. Naser." But you can still see the scar here on my throat. He cut me here and here. He stuck his knife in here. MR. DI FAZIO: For the purposes of the record, if Your Honours please, the witness indicates just under his jawbone on his right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That period of time that we're talking about up to the 6th February, did you see Mr. Zulfo Tursunovic at this new location, the place near the municipality building?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember how often he came?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Zulfo came nearly every day. We got to know him in those 46 days. Hardly a day wouldn't go by that he didn't come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell the Trial Chamber what he did when he visited.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When he arrived on one occasion on the 6th in the evening, three times they beat him and I asked Mr. Zulfo several times, "Why don't you kill us and stop torturing us?" And he replied, "Mr. Naser will decide about that and our government." And on the 6th in the evening, on the 7th of Sunday I remember well we asked what day it was and he passed through our cell, our room. And when he saw Kostadin Popovic dead and stiff and this elderly man who was over 65 from Skelani, from Rasica Gaj, he said, "It's easy to beat you here in the room. They should go to the forest and catch the fighters. You're no kind of fighters," but then two men arrived with a stretcher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get to the beating on the 6th in just a while. In the period of time that you were in prison, did you ever -- were you ever let out of prison to conduct jobs or chores?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever go into the women's prison, the women's cells?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the reason that you found yourself in the women's cell?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They took us there two by two to the municipality to bring firewood to the women so that they could burn the firewood. On three or four occasions I went to bring them wood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you get to see the women in their cell?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see if there were any children there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember who the kids -- who the children were? I don't necessarily mean their names but can you remember what sex they were and how old they were?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I couldn't see, but I think they were boys. I don't know. They were wearing trousers and the caps on their heads. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall how many children or young, very young, teenagers?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Four. There was a little Branko from Bjelovac. Both his parents were killed. He was about 7, and the others were a bit younger than Branko. The guards would call out to him. He would come to our cell and they would call him Branko by name. He was about 7. The others were younger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the men have wood and heating for their cell?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now let's turn to the 6th of February. You've told us that on that occasion the women were exchanged plus Stanoje.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already said in evidence that you were beaten that day -- you've already said in evidence that you were beaten that day. About what time did this beating take place?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This 6th of February when they exchanged 14 women and four children, during the night, I don't know exactly what time it was, two unknown men entered the cell and they took us to the duty room. I don't know whether the police or somebody else was on duty there for us prisoners. They took us out one by one and beat us and then they brought men back to our cell unconscious. I don't know what time I woke up in the night. They took us to a room and stripped us to the waist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's what I wanted to know. You were stripped to the waist and this was outside of your cell?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall much of the beating that you suffered?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I remember all my ribs on this side were broken. I have the letter of discharge when I was exchanged. All my ribs on many side. They kicked me, stamped on me with their feet, I was covered in bruises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you eventually lose consciousness?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you? In what position did you find yourself when you regained consciousness?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was in the cell where we were incarcerated. When it got light, I saw Kostadin Popovic lying next to me, and he was dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want to know is: Tell the Trial Chamber the position in which you found yourself when you regained consciousness. Where were the other men? Where were the other men in the cell? Were they all around the walls of the cell or were they positioned differently?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, we were unconscious. When we woke up we didn't know -- there were no lights. We had no watches. When they took us in, they brought a bucket with sand and there was an iron bar, around which there were leather thongs and they used that to see -- they would bring us back to the room and they would then splash cold water on us. Srebrenica was very cold. It was 10 below 0 at night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was this device that you've mentioned, the iron bar with the leather thongs? Is that an instrument of attack or is that some sort of lighting device? I'm just not clear about that.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It was used for lighting because there was no electricity so they used that to bring light in so that they could see to beat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyway, you regained consciousness, as I understand your evidence, in your cell?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When day came, were you able to see around -- inside the cell?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see Kostadin and the old man?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Kostadin and the old man look like?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, Kostadin was all covered in blood, and the old man -- I don't know. I didn't come close but perhaps I can show the Chamber so they can see. There's a photograph when his body was dug up his jaw was still black and blue and his teeth had been knocked out. I have Kostadin's picture to show.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we do -- I didn't realise the photograph was about to be produced. We would object to that because, firstly, we have no idea when the photograph was taken, no details of the exhumation, and how this witness would even know that that is Mr. Popovic. I believe there's witnesses who will deal with this. MR. DI FAZIO: I see the witness is thumbing through his well-used book that he's transported all the way here in which he's tried show me. I'm not going to need evidence of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. I think we'll have a break now of 25 minutes. More or less minus the time we consumed in the beginning and earlier on, you've been already about two and a half hours with this witness, just under two and a half hours. How much more time do you require? MR. DI FAZIO: I've got to get through this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I'm asking. MR. DI FAZIO: Just let me ... Actually not that much more. We can deal with him in about 45 minutes, 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 45 minutes. Basically it's the next session. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't think there's any doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So more or less, Mr. Jones, it's tomorrow for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which brings us back to what we discussed in the beginning, make sure that we don't get two persons here waiting the entire week until Friday -- until Monday of next week and today week, at least one of them should stay home. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll go through the list this afternoon, as I said, and I'll give you a new list tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. But as I understood from the registrar, two are here and two are coming today. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I don't have the facts at my fingertips. If that's happened, Your Honour, there's nothing I can do about that -- that situation. That's just it. I've heard about what you've said about getting people here too far in advance and I'll see if we can rectify any developing problems like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One or both may stay home probably. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, let's proceed and finish with this witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. If Your Honours please, I -- just on that very topic, when I gave you my assessment I forgot that there was a video that I want to show and some photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I've seen it on my -- not the video but I've seen a reference that you were intending to show the witness a video. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, in fact, there's a couple of videos. They're not long. One is more of a location video, the places in Srebrenica and so on. I'll fast forward for that for most of it. That will either take us right up to the line or possibly cross over. But -- for tomorrow. If I do have to go into tomorrow, it will only be a matter of minutes, literally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, more or less that you followed the main part of the direct. How much time you think you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Roughly two, and a half or three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically, more or less have the other witness in line tomorrow. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you'll start with the other witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Be waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You'll have as much time as you require, Mr. Jones. I'm not restricting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nikolic, I want to ask you some questions. You've given a description of the beating on the night of the 6th. Did you see Mr. Zulfo Tursunovic following that beating?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the bodies of Kostadin and the old man?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the evening when they were beaten on the 6th, at around 10.00 Zulfo Tursunovic arrived and walked through the cell in the prison. Kostadin and this elderly man were dead. He asked what had happened. We were all bloody. We were silent. We didn't answer. He -- later an unknown man arrived with a pencil and piece of paper and he asked if we knew their names and I said, Yes, this is Kostadin Popovic from Kravica. He wrote it down on a piece of paper. And they put it in Kostadin's pocket. When he was exhumed some people were exhuming bodies in Srebrenica and they found these piece of paper in his trousers. It hadn't rotted away because he was wrapped up in nylon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You've told us already that you were exchanged on the 27th of February, 1993. Following this beating on the night of the 6th of February, did you continue to be beaten or not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already told us the types of beatings that you suffered. Was there any change in the pattern following the 6th of February?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And were instruments used during those beatings after the 6th?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't recall everything. But nearly every day we were beaten, sometimes with fists. It's been 11 years now, so I've forgotten some things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You've described Mr. Naser Oric being one of the people who was with you when you -- in your journey following your capture. Did you -- after your capture on the 12th of January, 1993, did the man that you knew as Naser Oric, did you ever see him again?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were exchanged on the 27th of February --

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- 1993. How did it come about that you were exchanged? Were you consulted?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it simply happen to you? In other words, were you taken away for exchange?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: A man arrived in our cell. He looked around the room and he said, Two are to be exchanged. Nikolic, come on, and you and Ilija are going to be exchanged. You are on the list for exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that on the day of the 27th or prior to that day?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Before that they took us to be exchanged on two occasions and brought us back. This was at intervals of two or three days. And then finally we were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you exchanged? Where was the point at which you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It was Dragivote [phoen] above Skelani and Srebrenica, a place up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took you to the exchange point?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Three from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Men?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Ordinary clothes, simple clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following your exchange on the 27th, were you hospitalised?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown P45, please. I think this is one of the ones raised by Mr. Jones, one of the documents discussed earlier by Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Put your glasses on, Mr. Nikolic, so you can have a look at the document and read it carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just want to clarify that we did discuss this document, but it is one which we have objected to [Realtime transcript read in error: "not objected to"]. And I'll say no more at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to run quickly through the written details that you can see about certain people in this document. The man Jakov from Kalabaca, did you ever know his surname?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We learned it in Srebrenica when he came from Cerska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Incidentally, in the English text the family name, the surname, is not correct. It's just, for the record. I won't mention it -- mention the surname here because -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it's not correct. MR. DI FAZIO: All right. Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Branko Sekulic, you've mentioned his name as being one of the people in custody. Did he tell you where he was from?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Branko Sekulic was from Rogaci, that's the municipality of Vlasenica. He was in Cerska, in the barn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just cast your eye down those names, Sekulic; Dragan Ilic; Ratko Nikolic, we know that's you; and Ilija Ivanovic you've already spoken of. What about the next one? Milisav Milovanovic, who was that person?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He was known as Mico. His nickname was Mico.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you aware of anyone being in custody with you named Rado Pejic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Rado Pejic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you don't know, that's okay. I'm just asking you, was that -- was he one of the people in custody with you or not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me be clear about that. You don't know anyone --

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They were detained -- he was in hospital down there, and maybe he came up for a night, but he was taken back to the hospital. He wasn't with us. I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You don't know anyone going by the name Redo Pejic; is that your evidence? I'm not asking if it was the man who was brought up from hospital. I'm asking you a very simple thing. You don't know anyone by the name of Rado Pejic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Next name on the list, Milomir Djokic. Do you know anyone going by the name Milomir Djokic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He was a man from Zenica. He was in hospital. That evening he was with us. He was in hospital. He had been wounded near Kravica. He was there for only one night and then he was sent back. He remained in hospital when I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And of course you've already mentioned Kostadin Popovic. Do you -- did you know of anyone in jail, in custody with you called Bogdan Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That's the man, probably, who was beaten at the same time as Kostadin in the evening when they were beaten in the evening. At about 10.00 they were taken away. So probably that's the name of that man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, did a body called Committee for Mediation and Exchange ever consult with you, speak to you about you being exchanged prior to your exchange?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I just correct the transcript. I said this document, it's at page 80, line 20, that we did object it to it. I said we didn't discuss it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just wanted that on the record. Judge Eser would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I have a question to the Prosecution. If I'm correct, the exchange took place on the 26th of February, and the document which you just saw is from the 9th of February. Is there an explanation for this difference of dates? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, if Your Honours -- if Your Honour pleases, I'm pretty sure this witness can't give you an explanation, and as far as I'm aware, the Prosecution can't either at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: The background of my question is that people, while on this list of the 9th of February may not necessarily be identical with those who have been in fact exchanged on the 26th of February. Is that correct? As the list of the 9th of February, the names here -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Must not be necessarily identical with those people who have been exchanged on the 26th February -- MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, I see. I follow Your Honour's point. That's right. As I understand the evidence of this witness, he said two people on this list were exchanged with him, he mentioned their names, himself and Ilija Ivanovic. He didn't mention anybody else being exchanged on the 27th. I'm not saying this document represents in fact the number of people who were exchanged on that particular day, not on the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't even -- I suppose we don't even have evidence whether the others were actually exchanged or not. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. There are notations on the side of the document. I don't know what the significance of those are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know either. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn to your -- post-exchange, the events after your exchange. You were taken to hospital. How much did you weigh when you were taken to hospital?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think -- well, it's in my letter of discharge. About 70 or 75 kilos, or maybe less than 50 kilogrammes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, okay -- if you don't know how much you weigh, can you tell the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a little bit of a difference between 70 and 75 and 50. MR. DI FAZIO: I think there is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. MR. DI FAZIO: What I'll do is I'll ask -- perhaps if I can deal with it in this way, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you lose weight while you were in prison?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber as best you can -- I don't need exact kilos -- but was it a lot of weight or did you lose just a little weight? What condition were you in?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I lost over 20 kilogrammes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. How long did you remain in hospital?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: From the 12th of January to the 26th of February. On the 27th I was exchanged, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just think carefully about my question. I'm asking about the period of time after you were released, after you were exchanged. You said that you went to hospital. Now, how long were you in hospital after you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: A little longer than -- well, I think 16 days, and then they sent me home to recover. They told me to stay in bed. You can see the dates of my admittance to hospital and my discharge on the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you treated for broken ribs?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the cut that you mentioned on the side of your jaw? Were you treated for that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. They cleaned it out -- they cleaned out my teeth, however the cut on my throat had already healed. There was just the scar left but they cleaned out my right jaw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you lose teeth?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You keep touching one of your teeth at the front of your mouth. Is that the tooth that's loose that still remains loose to this day?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: From Srebrenica until today. I asked the doctors to take it out but they said, Leave it in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Following these events in 1993, were you ever filmed for television or any sort of programme at all involving filming yourself?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, once. Banja Luka TV.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you remember approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you first arrived at The Hague, did I show you an excerpt from a film in which you appeared?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had an opportunity to see it. Is that the film that was taken in Banja Luka or is that some other film? Or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, it's not the film in Banja Luka? Or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. I know that once people from Banja Luka TV came to my home to see me there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you an excerpt from a video and if just you -- I want you to have a look at and tell us if you see yourself depicted. MR. DI FAZIO: And if Your Honours please, firstly before it occurs, just for the purposes of the transcript I need to get the exhibit number of that. Thank you. If Your Honours please, for the purposes of the transcript it's Exhibit P448 that I wish to show to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. All right. MR. DI FAZIO: I have copies, if Your Honours please, of that transcript that was prepared from last time we discussed this. Do I get to keep one? I'll just get those distributed and then show the film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm being informed, Mr. Di Fazio, that although it has been premarked, it has not been exhibited, this video clip. MR. DI FAZIO: The transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, not the transcript. It's the video which has been premarked and not yet exhibited. Am I correct? MR. DI FAZIO: That's right. I'm now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It has been premarked P448 but it has not yet been tendered in other words. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes, yes, I understand. I think that will probably happen through Racine Manas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's something that can be solved very easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As far as the transcript is concerned we actually prepared a corrected version of the transcript for this witness because we don't accept that this is actually an accurate translation. It's not a matter which necessarily has to be dealt with now but we'll be dealing with the same extract tomorrow so we have our own version of this transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. MR. DI FAZIO: I won't have any questions about the substance of this. So ... Thank you. Now, if we could show Mr. Nikolic the excerpt that starts at 15:51 and ends at 18:58.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Nikolic, can I ask you to look at the screen and tell us if that's yourself?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: It would be good to have some sound. Is there any particular reason why haven't got the sound? It doesn't receive sound? Well, I can deal with this fairly quickly. As I said, I'm not going to ask for any questions regarding the content. If Mr. Jones needs to do that for tomorrow -- intends to do that tomorrow, perhaps if he can let us know and we can make arrangement to ensure that next time it's shown, if it's shown, there is sound accompanying it. But all I need to know -- ask the witness is this:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that you can see there in the film, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And did you watch that in my office the other day?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you talking there about these events in early 1993 that we've been talking about today?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber if you've got any idea at all when that film was shot. If you can't say, just tell us. If you can tell us, tell us.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the -- what I suspect is Cyrillic lettering at the top left-hand corner, do you recognise that? Does that give you any clue or not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know what these letters mean, ZB.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Good. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It must be some sort of a TV reference. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you very much. MR. DI FAZIO: I've finished with that exhibit. I now want to show the witness a number of photographs, please. They will be photographs that come from Exhibit P419.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally the English text of the script relating to this video which we were handed do you want to tender that into evidence, Mr. Di Fazio, or not? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I'm in Your Honours' hands on that. But we've asked for a formal translation to be done and it was used during the course of submissions as well. I wonder if the earlier transcripts when we had submissions on this -- on the whole video you recall last week, whether they were marked for identification on that occasion or not. I don't recall if they were. If they weren't, then, yes, I would ask that this the document be marked for identification at the very least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, I put the question to Mr. Di Fazio precisely because of what you said earlier. My instinct tells me that it should be admitted into evidence especially if tomorrow you're going to contend that this translation is not correct, because how are we going to make comparisons or some to a conclusion if it isn't?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour, and we will be tendering our version tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this will be P448.1, P448.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: This is just a draft, of course, this translation. And as I said, we're asking for the official translation to be prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, these photos that you are going to show the witness, again, they have again been premarked but not yet tendered. MR. DI FAZIO: No. They are part of a bundle which is made up of Exhibit P419.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
